name: Kinematic Video and Generated Movement
title: Kinematic Video and Generated Movement
answer: Kinematic video and generated movement covers systems that turn recorded or synthetic motion into video, notation, or interactive choreography. It includes pose estimation from live or archival footage, motion capture retargeting onto digital bodies, and generative video models that produce dance or physical action from text, music, or keyframes. The work sits between choreography, animation, and computer vision, and it is used for rehearsal tools, performance design, and movement analysis. This atlas tracks 1000 video models, a portion of which are capable of kinematic output.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard GPU workstations and cloud instances for training and inference, with real-time use often requiring local acceleration. Motion capture systems, depth cameras, and ordinary video feeds provide input, while pose estimation libraries and skeletal solvers convert that input into joint data. Generative video models are typically large diffusion or transformer networks, and they are served through APIs or local checkpoints. Datasets of motion capture, dance notation, and labeled video are the main fuel.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common pipeline starts with extracting 2D or 3D keypoints from video, then mapping those keypoints to a rigged body or a latent motion representation. Generative models learn motion priors from large collections of movement data and can be conditioned on text, music, or a starting pose to produce new sequences. Choreographers often work iteratively, generating short clips, selecting usable phrases, and retargeting them onto different performers or avatars. Some tools convert between video, Labanotation, and other movement scores, though this conversion remains approximate.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main rights questions are performer consent, likeness, and choreographic authorship. Training data often includes recordings of dancers whose movement signatures can be reproduced without their ongoing involvement, and provenance is rarely documented at the clip level. The atlas tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits; these cases are not specific to choreography, but they shape how courts treat training data and generated output. Risk also includes deepfake use of a person's body and the erasure of credit for choreographic labor.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward real-time tools that let a choreographer sketch movement with a camera or a few keyframes and receive generated variations immediately. Better physics, contact, and weight transfer are likely to make generated movement less floaty and more usable for stage and screen. Integration with notation systems and archival motion libraries may allow search and recomposition across historical dance recordings. As consent and provenance tooling improves, the field may settle into a practice where generated movement is treated more like a licensed performance asset than a raw model output.
